visits.text: The Kiruna→Abisko road (95 km) runs along Lake Torneträsk, Scandinavia's largest mountain lake – 330 km² of glacial water framed by peaks. In clear weather, you'll glimpse Lapporten (Čuonjávággi in Northern Sami), the U-shaped glacial valley that's one of Lapland's symbols.

Abisko National Park, founded in 1909, covers 77 km². Start at the Naturum, the park information centre. In the afternoon, follow the Abiskojåkka canyon trail – allow an hour for the short route there and back. The river has carved a deep gorge in the rock. Climb towards the mountains from Abisko Turiststation for the most impressive viewpoints.

From Abisko Turiststation, follow the Kungsleden – the King's Trail, which crosses Swedish Lapland all the way to Hemavan. For a hike of a few hours, walk the first section through birch forest and along the Abiskojåkka, then turn back whenever you wish. Experienced hikers can continue to Lake Abiskojaure, about 14 km from Abisko: the roughly 28 km round trip then makes for a long day of hiking. Bring good footwear and equipment suitable for rapidly changing weather.

Third day in Abisko – take your time. You've driven for two weeks to get here; now it's time to catch your breath. The wooden sauna by Lake Torneträsk (book at Abisko Turiststation that morning) is one of the journey's most memorable experiences – especially if you alternate sauna sessions with a plunge into the glacial lake.

activities.text: If you're here from September to March, the Aurora Sky Station on Mount Nuolja is the place to go in the evening. Chairlift to 900 m, panoramic terrace and heated café. Abisko benefits from a microclimate called the “blue hole”: the mountains create a clear-sky zone even when it's raining in Kiruna. In summer, the same chairlift takes you up to see the midnight sun. Book ahead.

If you prefer a short and easy hike, follow the loop along the Abiskojåkka from Abisko Turiststation. Over roughly 3.5 km, the trail crosses birch forest and follows the river and its canyon, with several viewpoints over the national park landscape. Take time to observe the local birds and Arctic vegetation: it is an excellent alternative for enjoying Abisko without setting out on a long day of walking.

In summer, guided hikes to the summit of Nuolja (1,164 m) depart in the evening from the Aurora Sky Station to see the midnight sun. In winter, this is where you have the best chance of seeing the northern lights on the entire trip. Otherwise, rest, read, wander freely – Abisko is a place where doing nothing is perfectly legitimate.

visits.text: Åre is Sweden's main mountain resort – and one of Scandinavia's most important. In winter, it's the country's most popular alpine ski area, host of the Alpine World Ski Championships (1954, 2007, 2019). In summer, the crowds vanish and the village returns to a human scale: a few lively streets, restaurants, a central square where hikers and mountain bikers mingle.

The Kabinbanan cable car climbs in 7 minutes from the central square (421 m) to the upper station at 1274 m – 853 m elevation gain in cabins accommodating 75 people. From the station, an additional 30-minute walk leads to Åreskutan summit (1420 m) and Toppstugan – Sweden's highest café, operating since 1892, where they serve waffles without running water or electricity (everything is carried up by hand). The panorama from up there over Jämtland's ranges is the perfect endpoint for this circuit.

The village of Fröå Gruva, east of Åreskutan, marks the site of an old mine surrounded by hiking and cross-country ski trails. A little away from the main tourist routes, it's a quiet way to end the day before catching the train.

activities.text: Åre is renowned for downhill mountain biking – the lifts operate in summer to take riders uphill. Local operators offer bike hire and downhill lessons. If you're not a mountain biker, the marked hiking trails around the massif offer 5–15 km loops with beautiful views over Lake Åresjön below.

Åre is connected by train to Östersund (1 hour) and Stockholm (6 hours 30 minutes), as well as to Storlien and Norway to the west (30 minutes to the border). If you continue to Norway, the train journey through the Jämtland valley is one of the country's most beautiful – plan to sit by the window.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Borgholm Castle is an imposing ruin atop a rocky plateau overlooking the sea. Begun in the 16th century and expanded until the 18th, it burned in 1806 and was never rebuilt. Its ochre sandstone walls and gutted towers have a romantic allure. The interior is open to visitors, and summer concerts are held here.

Solliden Royal Palace, the Swedish royal family's summer residence since 1906, has gardens that are partly open to visitors. The private apartments remain closed, but the French-style parterres and flower-filled terraces are worth visiting.

Stora Alvaret is a limestone steppe extending over 260 km² in the centre and south of the island. This almost lunar landscape - short grass, exposed rocks, wild orchids in spring - is one of the rare examples of this ecosystem in Europe. It earned Öland its UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2000. From Borgholm, allow for a day trip to explore the plateau and return.

The Ottenby bird reserve, at the southern tip of the island, is one of Scandinavia's most important migration sites. More than 300 species have been recorded here. At the end of the headland, Långe Jan - “Long John” - is Sweden's tallest lighthouse at 41 metres. From Borgholm, allow for a day trip to visit the reserve and lighthouse and return.

Öland has several hundred windmills, including around forty still standing along the east coast. The most accessible are around Lerkaka, where five windmills stand side by side in a meadow. From Borgholm, allow for a round trip by road to Lerkaka.

activities.text: Öland is completely flat - it is the ideal island for cycling. Rental shops in Borgholm offer bicycles for exploring southwards. The cycle path follows the east coast for several dozen kilometres.
Birdwatching at dawn at Ottenby: in spring and autumn, the migrations of cranes, geese and birds of prey are spectacular from sunrise. From Borgholm, allow for the round trip by road for this outing.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Funäsdalen is the hub of life in mountainous Härjedalen: a mountain village at the foot of Funäsdalsberget, surrounded by over 30 peaks exceeding 1000 m in the area. The Härjedalens Fjällmuseum, inaugurated in 1999, is one of Sweden's most modern museums. Its beautiful exhibitions present the region's history through mountain farmers, Sami people and craftspeople – its collections are among the country's oldest. It received a special mention at the 2001 European Museum of the Year Awards.

Push on to Tännäs, about twenty kilometres east, to see the musk oxen at Myskoxcentrum. In 1971, five musk oxen spontaneously crossed the Norwegian border and settled in the mountains west of Tännäs – forming the basis of the current herd. The centre, created in 2010, offers guided visits at a respectful distance. These animals, covered in their thick woolly coats, look like something out of prehistory – because that's exactly what they are. Book ahead.

activities.text: Funäsdalsberget (the mountain just above the village) offers a half-day hike accessible to all. From the summit, the view extends as far as Sylarna in the north and Sonfjället in the south – a panorama taking in 30 peaks. In summer, the ski runs transform into marked trails.

Nordic Ski Center (NSC) at Funäsfjällen claims one of the world's longest groomed cross-country ski networks, with 300 km of trails. In summer, these same trails become mountain bike and hiking paths. Outfitters offer mountain bike rentals on-site.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Gällivare is a mining town of 10,000 inhabitants set in the tundra. The Aitik copper mine, 15 km to the south, forms a crater 3 km long and 450 m deep. Guided tours are available in summer. In Malmberget, the neighbouring mining village, the same phenomenon as in Kiruna is occurring: the ground is subsiding and part of the village is being relocated.

Dundret (820 m), the mountain overlooking Gällivare, offers a 360° panorama over forests, lakes and tundra. It's one of Lapland's best places to observe the midnight sun (late May to mid-July): a paved road climbs almost to the summit. In winter, Dundret is also an aurora viewing spot.

activities.text: Muddus National Park is one of Europe's last remaining primeval forests - 700-year-old pines, peat bogs and the Muddusfallet waterfall (a 42 m drop). Plan a return trip during the day from Gällivare to the car park. The walk to the waterfall (7 km one way) is worth the effort.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Gävle is the home of the Gävlebocken, the world's most famous straw Christmas goat. Every first Sunday of Advent since 1966, a giant goat standing 13 metres tall and made of 3.6 tonnes of straw has been erected. The problem: vandals regularly set it on fire before Christmas. In 2001, an American tourist burned it down, believing this was a legal tradition - he spent 18 days in prison. The goat even has its own Twitter account. If you visit in December, you will see it (perhaps).

Gamla Gefle is the old fishing quarter - colourful wooden houses from the 18th century, narrow lanes and a village atmosphere in the middle of the city. It survived the fire of 1869, which destroyed much of Gävle.

The Swedish Railway Museum (Sveriges Järnvägsmuseum) is the country's largest railway museum – 19th-century steam locomotives, royal carriages, and a reconstructed station from 1900. Even if you're not a train enthusiast, the exhibition design is worth the visit. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes.

activities.text: Boulognerskogen park, in the city centre, is one of northern Sweden's finest urban parks – tall trees, a river, and open-air concerts in summer. If you have the campervan, several parking areas are accessible on the city outskirts.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: The STF Grövelsjön Fjällstation stands at an altitude of 816 m on the slopes of Långfjället, at the northern tip of Dalarna, right beside the Norwegian border. It's one of the STF (Swedish Tourist Association) mountain stations – with accommodation, a restaurant and a shop. Settle in: you're at the gateway to an exceptional hiking area with few visitors.

Lake Grövelsjön itself stretches like a banana for 15 km, straddling the Swedish-Norwegian border – its northern end lies in Norway. From Sjöstugan, 1.5 km from the mountain station, a boat crosses to Sylen on the Norwegian shore (a crossing of about 40 minutes). You'll pass into Norway without noticing – the border runs right through the middle of the lake.

The Linnaeus Trail (Linnéstigen) starts from Sjöstugan and climbs towards Norway following the exact route taken by botanist Carl Linnaeus in 1734 during his journey through Dalarna. On Långfjället, a sign marks the spot where Linnaeus observed falconers capturing wild falcons to train them for hunting – a remnant of a falconers' camp whose ruins still survive.

activities.text: The hike to the summit of Storvätteshågna (1204 m) is the day's major excursion – the highest point in Svealand, with a dizzying panorama over Norwegian fells, Töfsingdalen and the Helags massif to the north. Expect a 24 km round trip from the mountain station, taking roughly 7–8 hours. If you leave at 8am, you have plenty of time. The final ascent from Fosksjöarna is the steepest section.

For a more relaxed day, take the morning boat from Sjöstugan to Sylen (Norway), then walk back via the Linnaeus Trail (9 km back along the lake, easy terrain). You “enter” Norway without a passport, without customs, without anything – just a name change on the map. Silverfallet, a pretty waterfall 7 km from the mountain station, is an even shorter alternative.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Idre is a small village set close to the Norwegian border in northwestern Dalarna. The surrounding region is fjäll country – those bare high plateaus above the treeline characteristic of Scandinavia. Take time to drive slowly as you arrive: the landscape shifts gradually from dense forest to bare, windswept ridges.

Städjan-Nipfjället Nature Reserve is worth a detour. Nipfjället reaches 1,192 m, and the 16 km² reserve was created in 1974 (expanded in 2010) to protect unique Arctic flora and fauna: reindeer, foxes and many species of mountain birds of prey. The distinctive, volcano-shaped silhouette of nearby Städjan (1,131 m) can be seen from afar.

activities.text: The circular hike up Städjan (6 km, ~380 m elevation gain) from the Nipstugan car park is the region's flagship excursion. The 360° panorama from the summit takes in Norwegian fells to the west and Dalarna's forests to the east. Allow 2.5–3 hours. The trail is well marked but the terrain is rocky on the upper section – good walking shoes are essential.

Shorter alternative: the ascent to Lillnipen (1100 m), starting from the upper Nipfjället car park, 1.5 km round trip. Very easy, perfect if you just want to feel the fjäll wind without exertion. The view over the Härjedalen fells to the east and Fulufjället to the west is well worth the minimal effort.

Idre Fjäll, the ski resort a few kilometres north of the village, offers 25 marked mountain bike trails in summer including the famous Städjan DH (rated black). Outfitters rent equipment on-site. It's one of Sweden's best-known MTB parks.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Just before Jokkmokk, you cross the Arctic Circle on the E45 – a signposted roadside marker where you can take photos. North of this line, the sun doesn't rise in winter and doesn't set in summer.

Ájtte Museum is Sweden's national museum of Sami culture. Its name means “storehouse” in Lule Sami. You'll see exhibitions on Sami nomadic life, reindeer herding, joik (Sami singing), ceremonial drums and costumes. It's Sweden's most comprehensive Sami museum. Allow at least 1 hour 30 minutes.

Jokkmokk's winter market has been held from the first Thursday to the following Saturday in February since 1605 - more than 400 years without interruption. King Karl IX decreed the creation of markets in Lapland to collect taxes and spread Christianity. Today, 30,000 to 40,000 visitors descend on this town of 3,000 inhabitants for three days of Sami crafts and reindeer races on the frozen lake. If you are not here in February, the small red Sami church with its separate bell tower recalls this history.

activities.text: Jokkmokk is the gateway to Laponia, a 9,400 km² UNESCO site comprising Muddus, Padjelanta, Sarek and Stora Sjöfallet national parks. Local operators offer guided outings in the boreal forest around the village.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Kalmar Castle is one of Sweden's best-preserved Renaissance castles. Here in 1397 the Kalmar Union was signed, a treaty uniting Sweden, Denmark, and Norway under a single crown—a union that lasted until 1523. The castle was remodeled in the 16th century by the Vasa kings, and its restored interior halls are among Scandinavia's most lavish.

Kalmar's baroque cathedral dates from the 17th century—built to plans by Nicodemus Tessin the Elder, the Swedish royal court architect. Its yellow facade and dome are recognizable from throughout the lower town.

Old Kalmar, rebuilt after a 17th-century fire, follows a regular grid plan with low wooden houses painted red, ochre, and yellow. Walk the Kalmarsund waterfront to see traditional boats moored facing Öland island.

activities.text: In the afternoon, cross the Öland Bridge—6 km of concrete over the sea, toll-free, opened in 1972 and still Sweden's longest bridge. The drive across with views of the Kalmarsund in good weather is an experience in its own right. You can stop on Öland for an initial look around before returning to spend the night in Kalmar.
The fishing establishments at Kalmar's harbor still serve fresh Baltic fish—perch, pike, and smoked eel are the local must-tries.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Karlskrona was founded in 1680 by King Charles XI as the main naval base for Sweden's Baltic fleet—the entire city was planned around its shipyards. It's the world's only still-operational baroque naval base, earning UNESCO World Heritage status in 1998. Start at the grand Stortorget, one of Sweden's largest baroque squares, flanked by two twin circular churches.

The Marinmuseum (Naval Museum) traces 350 years of Swedish naval history with models, cannons, uniforms, and a section on Baltic battles. Outside, you can board the submarine HMS Neptun, a real Cold War submarine open for tours—the passageways are narrow, the atmosphere claustrophobic, and it's fascinating.

The Admiralty Church (Amiralitetskyrkan), built in 1685, is the largest surviving wooden church in Sweden. Before its entrance stands a wooden statue of an old lighthouse keeper who has been begging since the 18th century—tradition calls for dropping a coin in his bowl.
Karlskrona's archipelago extends across dozens of islands and islets around the city. Local ferries reach the main inhabited islands from the central harbor—some shelter 18th-century fortifications.

activities.text: Rent a kayak from the harbor to paddle along the fortifications—the view of the city and bastions from sea level is very different from the view from the quays.
Karlskrona's covered market (Saluhallen) offers smoked Baltic fish, Swedish cheeses, and Scanian gingerbread—a good option for a quick lunch.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Kiruna's LKAB mine is the world's largest underground iron ore mine. Opened in 1899, it extracts ore at a depth of over 1,365 metres along a 4 km seam. Guided tours descend by bus to level 540 – 400 km of tunnels in total. Sweden is the European Union's top iron producer thanks to this deposit. Book ahead: places sell out quickly in high season.

Kiruna's wooden church (Kiruna Kyrka), built between 1909 and 1912 by Gustaf Wickman, draws inspiration from Sami tents and Norwegian stave churches. Weighing 672 tonnes, it was voted Sweden's most beautiful building constructed before 1950. In 2025, it was moved 5 km to escape the mining subsidence zone – the entire town is being relocated eastward.

Free day in Kiruna. The town's relocation is a spectacle in itself: 'new Kiruna', 3 km east, is growing around a new central square while the old centre gradually empties. Some historic buildings are moved on trailers – others demolished. You can observe the process from signposted viewpoints in town.

Jukkasjärvi, in addition to the Icehotel, is a historic Sami village with a 17th-century wooden church whose altarpiece is the work of Bror Hjorth. Operators offer Sami cultural visits with local reindeer herders.
Return Abisko→Kiruna (95 km). Last visits or shopping in Kiruna. If you haven't yet, climb to the LKAB mine viewpoint – the crater is visible from the road.

If you still have time before your flight, enjoy one last walk along the shore of Lake Luossajärvi near Kiruna. The open views across the water, surrounding hills and distant mining facilities capture the contrast that defines the town between Arctic nature and industrial activity. It is an easy stop to adapt to your departure time.

activities.text: The Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi (17 km east), rebuilt each winter since 1989 from Torne river ice, is the world's first ice hotel. The permanent section stays open year-round through refrigeration. An hour's visit suffices to appreciate the sculptures and ephemeral architecture.

For those feeling energetic, climb Luossavaara (775 m), the mountain north of Kiruna – a former iron mine converted to a ski resort. In summer, the view from the summit takes in the town, Lake Luossajärvi and Lapland's mountains.

Last evening in Lapland. If you are travelling by campervan, choose an authorised place for your final night, ideally beside a lake or in a natural setting around Kiruna. Allemansrätten gives considerable freedom to people travelling on foot or camping in a tent, but it does not give motor vehicles the right to drive or park anywhere in nature. Follow road signs and any local restrictions.
Departure from Kiruna airport (flights to Stockholm, approximately 1 hour 30 minutes). Return the campervan or car in Kiruna. The airport is 8 km from the city centre.

visits.text: The Flatruet road stops you in your tracks as soon as you leave the forest: you are at an altitude of 975 m, on Sweden's highest road, opened in 1938. Ahead lies a bare, windswept, treeless plateau - and reindeer on the road, indifferent to your car. Stop at the parking area on the crest: in clear weather, you can see Helagsfjället and its glacier to the north. The road is partly gravel and closes at night from December to mid-April.

Ljungdalen is a tiny village at the foot of Helagsfjället. It's the starting point for reaching STF Helags Fjällstation, a 12 km hike from the Kläppen car park (6 km by car from Ljungdalen). The mountain station is the base for the glacier ascent.

Helagsfjället (1,797 m) is Sweden's highest peak south of the Arctic Circle - and its slopes hold the Helags glacier, the southernmost in Sweden. The summit can be seen from afar: it dominates the surrounding landscape in spectacular fashion.

activities.text: The ascent of Helagsfjället from the mountain station is an 8 km round trip. From the summit at 1,797 m, the view extends to Sylarna in the north, Norway to the west and the Härjedalsfjällen in every direction. On the way up, you follow the southern edge of the glacier - a geological curiosity in the heart of Scandinavia. Allow 4 to 5 hours from the mountain station. Bring warm clothes even in summer: the weather changes very quickly here.

If you don't want to climb to the summit, the hike from Kläppen to the mountain station (12 km one way, Kesudalen valley and birch forest) is already very beautiful. You can stay overnight at the mountain station and return the next day. Book ahead: there are few places.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Gammelstad kyrkstad is the world's best-preserved church town, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1996. At the centre, the stone church of Nederluleå dates from the 15th century. All around, 424 small red wooden houses (Falun red paint) were built by farmers from surrounding parishes to sleep in at weekends – distances and climate made it impossible to return home after mass. In the 17th century, isostatic rebound made the harbour too shallow for ships – the trading town moved to the coast and took the name Luleå, leaving the religious complex intact.

The visitor centre's guided tour lasts about an hour and opens doors normally closed to the public. When you're not on a tour, wander freely through the lanes between the red houses: the place is still inhabited during religious festivals like Christmas and Easter.

activities.text: The Luleå archipelago has over 1,300 islands – in summer, boats serve the main ones. Gammelstadsviken nature reserve, right next to the church town, is one of northern Sweden's best spots for observing migratory birds.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Start with Västra Hamnen, the former industrial port transformed into a model residential district in the 2000s. This is where the Turning Torso stands: 190 metres of twisting white concrete, designed by Santiago Calatrava and inaugurated in 2005.

Stortorget, Malmö's main central square, is framed by the 16th-century city hall and the governor's residence. Head down to Lilla Torg, the small cobbled square lined with half-timbered houses where locals gather in the evenings—it's one of the city's liveliest squares.

Malmöhus Castle dates from 1434—it's the oldest surviving Renaissance castle in Scandinavia. Today it houses several museums: natural history, art, and a section devoted to the city's history. Allow at least 1.5 hours.

The medieval old town, centered around Stortorget and Sankt Petri Cathedral (14th century), deserves an hour of wandering. Behind its austere facade, the church conceals a 16th-century Flemish altarpiece and a burial crypt.

activities.text: Late in the day, head to the Ribersborg baths: a long wooden pier extending into the sea with gender-separated bathing cabins dating from 1898. Even out of season, regulars plunge into the cold waters of the Øresund.
Walk through Möllevångstorget, the local market in the southern district, to see Malmö away from the tourist routes: vegetable stalls, spice aromas, neighborhood cafés.

days_plan.itin_title: The Grand South: From Malmö to Stockholm via the Islands

visits.text: Lake Siljan spreads before you like an inland sea – 350 km² formed 377 million years ago by a meteorite impact, making it one of Europe's largest impact craters. Its shores are lined with wooden houses painted in dark red (the famous Falu rödfärg, a paint made from copper pigments extracted from the Falun mine) – the most quintessentially Swedish tableau imaginable.

The Zornmuseet holds the world's largest collection of works by Anders Zorn (1860–1920), a Mora-born painter who created portraits of three American presidents – Grover Cleveland, William Taft and Theodore Roosevelt. Don't miss Zorngården, his house preserved exactly as it was when his wife Emma died in 1942: guided tours in English run at 3pm Tuesday to Sunday. Allow 1.5 hours for both.

In Nusnäs, a few kilometres from Mora, you'll find the workshops where the famous Dalecarlian horses (Dalahäst) are hand-carved and painted – Sweden's unofficial symbol for generations. The craftspeople work before your eyes; it's much livelier than a museum.

On Mora's main square stands the Vasaloppet finish gate – the line that 15,000 cross-country skiers reach every first Sunday in March after 90 km from Sälen. A statue commemorates Gustav Vasa, whose ski escape in 1520 inspired the race. In 1521, the people of Mora had initially refused to join him, before changing their minds and catching up with him in Sälen to launch the uprising against the Danes.

activities.text: Cycle around Lake Siljan (Siljansleden, around 310 km for the full circuit - choose one section) or rent a kayak to paddle on its calm waters. In summer, several beaches are suitable for swimming: Siljansbadet in Rättvik is one of the best; plan a round trip by car during the day from Mora. Local providers offer rentals.

If you are here in late June, do not miss Midsommar: Dalarna is the beating heart of Sweden's Midsummer celebrations. In Leksand, on the lakeshore, more than 30,000 people gather around the leafy maypole every year - one of the country's largest celebrations. Plan a round trip by car during the day from Mora.

In the evening, stroll through central Mora – barely 10,000 inhabitants, yet packed with cafés, restaurants and craft shops. It's also the starting point of the Inlandsbanan, the legendary train that runs 1,300 km through Sweden all the way to Lapland.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

places.name: Ornskoldsvik

visits.text: The High Coast (Höga Kusten), listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000, is the site of the world's greatest post-glacial rebound: 20,000 years ago, 3 km of ice weighed down this land, pushing it down by 800 metres. Since the ice melted, the land has been rising by 8 mm a year - new islands regularly emerge. The High Coast suspension bridge (1,867 m), on the E4, is your gateway. From Örnsköldsvik, allow for approximately 83 km, a 1-hour drive to the bridge.

Skuleskogen National Park, established in 1984, is where this geological phenomenon is most visible. Slåttdalsskrevan is its centrepiece: a cleft 200 metres long and 40 metres deep in the red granite. The interior feels like a cathedral - the walls rise on either side and light filters down from above. Plan a return drive from Örnsköldsvik to the south entrance (Docksta), then allow 1 hour 30 minutes for the walk to the gorge and back. If you climb to the summit of Slåttdalsberget (280 m), the view over the archipelago is one of Sweden's most beautiful.

activities.text: Before or after your hike, stop at Naturum Höga Kusten at the foot of Skuleberget: the exhibition clearly explains isostatic rebound. From Örnsköldsvik, allow for approximately 36 km, a 25-minute drive. Bring sturdy footwear - the terrain is rocky and some sections are slippery.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

map_keywords: Skuleskogen national park entrance south Docksta

visits.text: Östersund is the only real city on the entire circuit – 60,000 inhabitants, capital of Jämtland, founded in 1786 by King Gustav III on the shores of Storsjön. It's a jolt of modernity after the fells: cafés, restaurants, street life. Take an hour to stroll along the lake before visiting.

Jamtli is Jämtland's regional museum, 1 km north of the centre. It combines an indoor museum with an exceptional collection – including the Överhogdal tapestries, discovered 50 km north of Sveg, parts of which date back to the 9th century and constitute Europe's best-preserved Viking tapestries – and an open-air museum with historic buildings from the 18th and 19th centuries where actors in period costume have recreated peasant life every summer since 1986. The Storsjöodjuret exhibition includes the giant trap built in 1894 to capture the beast, baited with a live pig.

The island of Frösön, linked to Östersund by a bridge, is Jämtland's historic heart, long predating the city. It holds Sweden's northernmost runestone, erected between 1050 and 1080 – and the monster carved on the stone is supposed to represent the Storsjöodjuret. Legend says a wizard named Ketil Runske imprisoned the beast in the stone with a spell. Frösön church (late 12th century) has a separate bell tower typical of Jämtland – the view over Östersund and the lake from the island is the region's finest.

Along the shores of Storsjön, Storsjöodjuret statues punctuate a pleasant walk. The creature was first mentioned in writing in 1635. In 1986, for Östersund's bicentenary, it was even placed under legal protection – a law repealed in 2005. There are now 200 documented testimonies from people claiming to have seen it.

activities.text: In summer, Storsjön lends itself to kayaking and stand-up paddling – outfitters offer rentals and outings from Badhusparken. In calm weather, paddling on the lake while watching Östersund's silhouette reflected in the water has something quite surreal about it.

Östersund has been a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy since 2010 – remarkable for a city this size. In the evening, try the restaurants in the centre showcasing Jämtland products: game, mountain cheeses, wild herbs. It's the circuit's only real “city” evening.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: At Berga By, a small, unassuming sign marks the official starting line of the Vasaloppet – the 90 km that have connected Sälen to Mora since 1922. The inaugural race on 22 March 1922 brought together 119 skiers starting from here; the course record now stands at 3 hours 28 minutes. Setting foot on this starting line gives a tangible sense of the distance the cross-country skiers are about to cover.

The Högfjällshotellet, built in 1937, is the oldest mountain hotel in the region – and one of Sweden's most popular. Even if you're not staying here, the architecture and the view from its terrace over the snow-covered slopes (or green slopes in summer) merit a stop.

activities.text: In summer, Vasaloppsleden becomes a hiking trail along the 90 km historic route between Sälen and Mora, with eight shelters along the way. You do not have to walk it all: choose a 10 to 20 km section from Sälen towards Smågan, the race's first refreshment station.

Sälen is also Sweden's largest alpine ski area, with several resorts clustered around the massif. In summer, the pistes become mountain bike trails and local operators offer bike hire and guided descents. The region is far less crowded than in winter – make the most of it.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Sara Kulturhus in Skellefteå is one of the world's tallest wooden buildings: 20 storeys, 75 metres, inaugurated in September 2021. Designed by White Arkitekter, the building is constructed almost entirely from regional timber (forests within 200 km, sawmill 60 km away). It houses a theatre, museum, art gallery, library and a 205-room hotel. The glass facade reveals the raw timber structure inside – go to the top floor for views over the forests and Baltic Sea.

Bonnstan is Skellefteå's medieval church town: 116 small red wooden cabins grouped around the parish church. As at Gammelstad (which you'll see further north), these houses were used by farmers from distant parishes who stayed overnight at weekends to attend mass. Bonnstan is smaller than Gammelstad but far less touristy – you'll likely be alone in the lanes.

activities.text: The banks of the Skellefte river, which flows through town, offer a pleasant evening walk. Nordanå cultural centre, on a former estate with wooden buildings by the water, hosts temporary exhibitions and a café overlooking the river. This is where the people of Skellefteå gather in summer.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: Welcome to Gamla Stan, the birthplace of Stockholm: the old town spreads across three islands - Stadsholmen, Riddarholmen and Helgeandsholmen - between Lake Mälaren and the Baltic Sea, exactly as it was in the 13th century when Birger Jarl founded the city here in 1252. The ochre and red facades dominating Stortorget, Stockholm's oldest square, once belonged to a medieval fortress. This same square was also the site of the 1520 Stockholm Bloodbath, one of Scandinavia's most infamous political massacres. Arrive early in the morning before the tour groups - the silence of the cobbled streets at dawn is worth as much as the monuments themselves.

At the heart of Gamla Stan, the Royal Palace (Kungliga Slottet) contains over 600 rooms and remains one of the official residences of the Swedish monarch. Built in the 17th and 18th centuries in baroque style, it houses several museums including the Royal Treasury and the Tre Kronor Museum. If you're here in summer, don't miss the changing of the guard - it takes place daily at 12:15pm and is accompanied in July-August by the military mounted band.

Get lost in Mårten Trotzigs Gränd, Stockholm's narrowest alley at just 90 centimeters at its tightest point, then stroll along Österlånggatan to wander past the Hanseatic houses that recall how German merchants controlled much of Baltic trade from these walls in the Middle Ages. In the evening, Stortorget becomes one of Stockholm's best spots to dine on a terrace facing the colorful facades.

Dedicate your morning to the Vasa Museum on the island of Djurgården. The Vasa was the most imposing warship of its era: 64 cannons, 700 sculptures, 1,200 tonnes. It sank on August 10, 1628, twenty minutes after leaving Stockholm harbor, after sailing just 1,300 meters. Salvaged 98% intact in 1961 after 333 years on the harbor floor, it's now the only 17th-century vessel preserved in the world. Allow at least 2 hours and arrive at opening (8:30am in summer) to see the ship without the tour group crowds.

After the Vasa, stay on Djurgården for Skansen, an open-air museum: 160 historic buildings dismantled across Sweden and rebuilt here, creating a miniature version of 19th-century Sweden. It is also a zoo with moose, lynx and reindeer. If the weather is on your side, the island deserves a long walk along the waterfront.

In late afternoon, head to Södermalm, Stockholm's bohemian district south of Gamla Stan. Climb to Monteliusvägen for one of the finest panoramic views of the old town at sunset - locals often gather here in the evening to enjoy the view. The neighborhood is filled with vintage shops, galleries and restaurants.

Tromsø→Stockholm flight (around 2 hours 30 minutes). Back in the Swedish capital, use these final hours to discover Östermalm, a more elegant side of Stockholm than the districts visited at the beginning of your trip. Walk along Strandvägen, the grand waterfront boulevard lined with late 19th-century buildings, then head to Östermalms Saluhall, the historic covered market where stalls selling fish, cured meats, cheeses and Swedish specialties also make it a good place for lunch.

City Hall (Stadshuset, 1923) on Kungsholmen island has hosted the Nobel Prize banquet every December 10 since 1930—in the Blue Hall, which isn't blue: architect Ragnar Östberg changed his mind at the last minute and kept the red bricks exposed, but the name was already printed on the plans. The guided tour tells this anecdote.

If you still have time before your departure, return to Djurgården for one last morning surrounded by greenery, just minutes from central Stockholm. Rather than revisiting places you have already seen, discover another side of this former royal hunting ground, now covered with parks, gardens and waterfront paths.

Still on Djurgården, ABBA The Museum tells the story of the Swedish group that became a worldwide phenomenon after winning Eurovision in 1974 with Waterloo. Stage costumes, gold records, personal objects and recreated studios feature throughout a highly interactive visit: you can, among other things, sing alongside avatars of the band and virtually try on some of their costumes.

East of Djurgården, the Museum of Ethnography (Etnografiska museet) houses collections devoted to the cultures of Africa, Asia, the Americas and Oceania. Ritual objects, textiles, sculptures and photographs also tell the story of explorers and Swedish ethnographic collections. A quieter and less crowded visit than the major museums in the city center.

If you are traveling with family or want to end your trip on a lighter note, Gröna Lund is Stockholm's historic amusement park, located on Djurgården's waterfront since 1883. Roller coasters, rides and attractions occupy a surprisingly compact space facing the old town. In summer, the park also hosts numerous open-air concerts.

For one last walk before leaving Stockholm, follow the Djurgårdsbrunn Canal through the most peaceful part of the island. The path follows the water between tall trees, small footbridges and old villas, away from the bustle of the museums. You can simply walk along the canal, then return toward the center according to the time you have before heading to Arlanda.

activities.text: Settle in and spend the evening dining in Gamla Stan or Södermalm—this is your first night in Scandinavia, so take your time. Tomorrow you'll have a full day in Stockholm before boarding the overnight train.

To understand why Stockholm is built on 14 islands, take a ferry from Nybroviken to Vaxholm (45 min) or the archipelago islands. In summer, some Stockholmers swim directly from the rocks. It's the best way to grasp that the city and water are one.

Tonight, board the SJ Nattåg 94 overnight train from Stockholm Central. Departure around 6pm, arrival at Abisko Östra the next day around 11am—17 hours of travel crossing all of Sweden from south to north. Book in advance: places go fast in aurora season and summer. You can choose between a seat in an open-plan car, a 6-berth couchette compartment, or a private cabin for 2–3 people. This train is a journey in itself—the landscapes between Kiruna and Abisko in the last hour are among the most beautiful of the journey.

Last evening in Stockholm: head to Fjällgatan, on the heights of Södermalm, to admire the lights of the old town, Djurgården and the islands surrounding the city center at twilight. This walk offers one last panorama of Stockholm before your departure day.
Departure from Stockholm. Arlanda airport is 40 minutes from the center by Arlanda Express from Stockholm Central. Plan to arrive 2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes before takeoff.

visits.text: Sundsvall is nicknamed Stenstaden – 'the Stone City'. On 25 June 1888, a spark from a steamboat on the Selångersån river triggered the largest urban fire in Swedish history: the entire city burned in nine hours, leaving 9,000 people homeless. The decision was made to rebuild everything in stone rather than wood. Result: 51 brick and stone buildings in neo-Renaissance style now line wide streets around Stora Torget. In 2017, Sundsvall was voted Sweden's most beautiful city.

The Kulturmagasinet, housed in four converted former harbour warehouses, contains the municipal library, Sundsvall Museum (city history and the fire) and a photography museum. It's the cultural heart of the city – free entry for most exhibitions.

Climb Norra Berget, the northern hill (141 m), for the panorama over the city, sea inlets and bridges. An open-air museum at the summit presents the region's history and culture. The trail from the centre is steep but short – 20 minutes' climb.

activities.text: In the evening, stroll through Stenstaden at sunset – the brick facades take on a golden hue. The fountain in Vängåvan park, created in 1886 (two years before the fire and miraculously intact), depicts lions, dolphins and bears – animals most Sundsvall residents of the time had never seen.

visits.text: You'll arrive in Sveg through seemingly endless forests – Härjedalen is Sweden's least populated province, and you feel it. At the main crossroads, you'll come straight upon it: the giant wooden bear standing 13 m tall, weighing 80 tonnes, built between 2003 and 2005 using 570,000 nails. It has become the symbol of the town and the entire province. The brown bear is Härjedalen's emblematic animal – and the province has one of Sweden's highest densities of brown bears.
Gammelgården in Sveg is an open-air museum run by the Härjedalen handicrafts association, founded in 1913. It brings together historic buildings from the region and presents local culture.

Sveg's Inlandsbanan station is a stop on the legendary line that connects Kristinehamn to Gällivare over 1,300 km through central Sweden. The Inlandsbanan only runs in summer (June-August), one train daily in each direction. If you're passing in July, go watch the train depart.

activities.text: Sonfjället National Park, 80 km north of Sveg, is worth an excursion. Plan a round trip by car during the day from Sveg. Its volcano-shaped silhouette can be seen from afar. It is one of Sweden's areas with the highest densities of brown bears - guides offer bear safaris at sunrise and sunset. Tracks are common even if you do not see the animal. Lilltoppen (around 1,000 m) can be reached without major difficulties from the northern entrance.

Alternatively, Björnberget, the local mountain 8 km from central Sveg, offers a pleasant half-day walk with views over Härjedalen's forests and hills. In the evening, Sveg is the sleepy provincial capital – 2,500 inhabitants – but the atmosphere is authentic, with no tourist artifice.

days_plan.itin_title: Wild Central Sweden: Dalarna, Härjedalen & Jämtland

visits.text: Umeå is nicknamed 'the City of Birches' – after a devastating fire in 1888 (the same day as Sundsvall's, 25 June), thousands of birches were planted as firebreaks. They still line the main avenues and give the city a unique appearance in autumn when the leaves turn yellow. With 90,000 inhabitants and a large university, it's northern Sweden's biggest city and served as European Capital of Culture in 2014.

Västerbottens Museum traces the region's history with emphasis on Sami culture and the forest industry. Outside, an open-air museum with old farms and buildings. Guitars – The Museum, opened in 2014, displays over 500 vintage guitars including pieces that belonged to famous musicians. Allow an hour per museum.

activities.text: Umeå has a surprisingly lively café scene for its latitude - students keep the city buzzing. Fika (a Swedish coffee break with a pastry) is almost a sport here. Walk along the Umeälven in the evening: the waterfront is lively in summer. If you have an extra half-day, the island of Norrbyskär reveals a former 19th-century sawmill village in an archipelago setting: allow for a drive from Umeå to the departure quay, followed by a boat crossing.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: On the way to Uppsala, stop in Sigtuna, Sweden's oldest town (founded around 980). From Uppsala, allow for approximately 31 km, a 35-minute drive. Its lanes beside Lake Mälaren, ruined medieval churches and runestones make it a worthwhile stop for a good hour. St Mary's Church, built in Gothic brick, is the best preserved.

Uppsala Cathedral, completed in 1435, is the largest church in Scandinavia – 118-metre neo-Gothic spires. Inside lie the tombs of Gustav Vasa and Carl Linnaeus. Facing the cathedral, the Gustavianum houses a 17th-century anatomical theatre and Anders Celsius's original thermometer.

Linnaeus Garden (Linnéträdgården) is the botanical garden Carl Linnaeus directed from 1743 to 1778 – here he developed his method for classifying living organisms. Linnaeus's adjoining house preserves his insect collections and notes. Allow an hour for both.

Gamla Uppsala, 5 km north, is the cradle of the Swedish nation. Three great royal burial mounds from the 6th century rise on a plain – climb the tallest for the view. A small 12th-century church was built on the foundations of an ancient pagan temple described in medieval chronicles.

activities.text: End the day by the Fyrisån river in central Uppsala – cafés with waterside terraces. If you're there on 30 April (Valborg), tens of thousands of students descend a hill throwing their white caps – a centuries-old tradition.

days_plan.itin_title: The Great Northern Journey: Stockholm to Lapland via the East Coast

visits.text: This morning, cross back over the Öland Bridge to the mainland, then drive north to Oskarshamn (~80 km from the bridge, about 1 hour). This is where the ferry departs for Gotland. Board a Destination Gotland ferry for a crossing of about 3 hours—book ahead in July–August, as spaces sell out quickly. Arrive in Visby by ferry from Oskarshamn. The first thing you'll see as you enter the harbor: the ramparts. These 3.4 km of medieval walls, built between the 12th and 14th centuries, rank among Northern Europe's best-preserved. UNESCO-listed since 1995, they feature 44 towers and have never been dismantled. Walk the complete circuit—allow 1.5 hours.

Visby's ruined medieval churches are among the town's most distinctive features. Gotland had 16 churches for a town of just a few thousand inhabitants in the Middle Ages—most were abandoned after 1361 when Danish King Valdemar Atterdag captured the city. The ruins of St. Catherine's (Franciscan, 13th century) and St. Nicholas are the most photogenic.

Fiskargränd, the “fishermen's lane,” is covered with blooming roses from June to August. It's one of Gotland's most photographed lanes—narrow, cobbled, with low houses whose gardens overflow onto the lane.

Gotland Museum (Gotlands Museum) holds the world's largest collection of painted rune stones—these slabs illustrated with mythological scenes date from the 5th to 11th centuries. The treasury section displays thousands of Viking-era coins found in the island's fields.

From Visby, head by road to the north of Gotland, then take the ferry to Fårö, the small island north of Gotland (free crossing, 5 minutes). This is where Ingmar Bergman lived and worked from 1967 until his death in 2007 - he filmed several works here, including Persona and Scenes from a Marriage. The house is visible from the outside; a centre devoted to his work organises screenings in summer. Plan this as a day trip with a return journey.

The raukar of Fårö are limestone columns sculpted by marine erosion over thousands of years. These strange formations, 3 to 6 metres high, stand on the island's beaches and heathland like petrified figures. The most accessible are at Langhammars and Digerhuvud. From Visby, allow for a day trip with a return journey by road and the ferry crossing to Fårö.

Gotland has more than 90 rural medieval churches, some dating back to the 11th century. They look similar from the outside - limestone walls, a square tower, interior paintings - but each hides different details. The churches at Gothem, Garde and Roma are among the most remarkable and can be visited freely. From Visby, allow for a round trip by road to Gothem and Garde.

activities.text: In the evening, Visby comes alive around Stortorget and the lanes of the center within the walls. Restaurants set up outdoor seating in the courtyards of medieval houses—it's an atmosphere quite different from the rest of Sweden.

If you arrive in summer (early to mid-August), check the dates of Visby's Medieval Week (Medeltidsveckan): it is one of Europe's largest medieval festivals, with costumes, jousting and markets throughout the old town.

From Visby, reach Fårö by road and then by ferry for this day trip. Rent a bicycle on Fårö to link the wild beaches and the raukar - the island is small (about 30 km long) and has few visitors. Sudersand is the most beautiful beach, with white sand and water that can reach 20°C in July.
Back in Visby in the evening, climb the northern ramparts to watch the sun descend over the Baltic Sea—in summer, light lingers until 10 PM.

visits.text: On the road between Malmö and Ystad, make a detour to Smygehuk: it is Sweden's southernmost point, marked by a small red-and-white striped lighthouse on a rocky coast. Nothing spectacular - but it is the country's geographical extremity. From Ystad, allow for a round trip by road for this visit.

Ystad is a well-preserved medieval town with cobbled lanes, tightly packed half-timbered houses, and a 13th-century Franciscan monastery, Klostret, now converted into a regional museum. Fans of the Wallander crime series will recognize the settings—exteriors were filmed here.

Do not miss Ales Stenar at Kåseberga, approximately 19 km from Ystad, a 20-minute drive to the village followed by a walk uphill to the monument. This megalithic monument of 59 standing stones forms a 67-metre ellipse shaped like a Viking ship on a grassy cliff facing the Baltic Sea. Built around AD 600, its exact purpose remains debated - a solar observatory, burial site, or commemorative monument. The sea view at sunset is one of the finest in Scania.

activities.text: Head up to the fishing village of Kåseberga at the foot of the cliff to see the boats hauled onto the shore and the traditional eel smokehouses - smoked eel is a local speciality. From Ystad, allow approximately 19 km, a 20-minute drive to the village.
In the evening in Ystad, walk along Stora Östergatan, the best-preserved street in the medieval center, and look for a café in one of the hidden courtyards behind the facades.
